title: Christine de Pizan Writes to Feed Her Family
text:
Christine de Pizan was born in Venice in 1364. Her father, a physician and astrologer, was called to the court of King Charles V of France and brought his family to Paris. Unusually for a girl, Christine was allowed to pick up learning at home. At fifteen she married Etienne du Castel, a royal secretary, and the marriage was happy.

Then, within a few years, her world collapsed. Her father died, and in 1390 her husband died suddenly in an epidemic. At twenty-five she was left with three young children, her widowed mother and a niece to support, and with debts she had known nothing about. She spent years in lawsuits trying to recover money owed to her husband's estate, and wrote later of the humiliation of being made to wait in courts and offices.

She decided to live by her pen. She began with poems of love and mourning, which found readers at court, and then moved on to history, politics and moral works. Rich patrons, among them the dukes of Burgundy and Berry, paid for copies, and she supervised the production of her manuscripts herself. She is often called the first professional woman writer in Europe. In The Book of the City of Ladies, in 1405, she defended women against the scorn of male authors.

In her Book of the Mutability of Fortune, she wrote that misfortune had changed her from a woman into a man, able to take the helm of her family's ship.
lesson: Loss can force us to discover abilities we never knew we had. Providing for those who depend on us can turn grief into purpose.
people: Christine de Pizan, Etienne du Castel
source: Christine de Pizan, Lavision-Christine (1405); The Book of the City of Ladies (1405); The Book of the Mutability of Fortune (1403)
